content.title: How to Watch ESPN2 Without Cable
content.text: Some links below are affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through them. ESPN2 always plays second fiddle to ESPN, but I know how important it is if you’re trying to follow college football, basketball, or even a big tennis match. It’s also the channel where ESPN stashes overflow games during the NBA Playoffs and Grand Slam tennis coverage. If you care about sports and want the full experience without a bloated cable bill, you need a reliable way to watch ESPN2. This time of year, ESPN2 leans heavily into live college sports. That usually means a steady mix of NCAA softball and baseball, along with NBA, NHL, and occasional soccer or fight cards filling out the schedule. At Antenna Land, my mission is to help you watch the TV you love without overpaying. While you can’t get ESPN2 with a TV antenna, you absolutely can use an antenna for your free local channels (like ABC, CBS, and FOX) with a lean streaming service to get the job done. That means ESPN2 requires a streaming plan, but an antenna still gives you free access to major games on ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX. This guide will walk you through all the best options to stream ESPN2, organized with the cheapest solutions first, so you can make the right choice for your cord-cutting setup. Editor’s Pick: ESPN UnlimitedThe cheapest way to get ESPN2 without a cable bundle. Includes ESPN, ESPN2 and the full ESPN channel lineup. See plans and start watching Can You Watch ESPN2 for Free? No. There isn’t a legal way to watch ESPN2 for free. ESPN2 is a cable channel. It’s tied to paid TV rights, so you need a subscription to a streaming service or cable replacement plan to watch it live. There are two practical ways to keep your costs down: You can use a short-term option like a Sling TV Day Pass or Weekend Pass if you only need ESPN2 for a specific game or event. Or you can build a cheaper setup by using a TV antenna for your local channels (ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC) and paying only for a smaller streaming service like ESPN Unlimited, which carries ESPN2. That second approach is how you avoid paying for a full cable bundle while still getting everything you need for sports. People sometimes get tripped up about direct ESPN subscriptions and free trials. ESPN Select (formerly ESPN+) does not include a live feed of ESPN2. It only carries separate live events and on-demand content. How to Watch ESPN2: A Breakdown of Your Best Options To solve the “how to watch ESPN2” problem, you need a streaming service, as it’s a cable channel unavailable with an antenna. Below, I’ve broken down each major service that carries ESPN2. Each section is a complete overview designed to help you decide which one best fits your needs and budget, from standalone sports packages to full cable replacements. Cheapest Way to Watch ESPN2 The cheapest way to watch ESPN2 depends on how often you actually need it. If you want full-time access, the ESPN Unlimited plan at $29.99 per month is the lowest-cost option that includes a live stream of ESPN2 and the rest of ESPN’s cable networks. If you only need ESPN2 for a game or a weekend, Sling TV is the cheapest route. Sling offers Day Passes starting at $4.99 and Weekend Passes for $9.99, which include ESPN2 through the Sling Orange lineup. For a regular monthly plan, Sling Orange at $45.99 per month is still one of the least expensive ways to keep ESPN2 in your channel lineup without paying for a larger bundle. If you’re watching every week, ESPN Unlimited is the simplest and cheapest long-term option. If you just need ESPN2 here and there, Sling’s passes are hard to beat. ESPN Unlimited For the most direct and comprehensive access to ESPN’s entire universe, the new ESPN Unlimited plan is your best bet. I have been using the Unlimited plan since it launched on August 21, 2025, and this standalone service is a no-brainer for sports fans who don’t want a larger bundle. A subscription costs $29.99 per month or $299.99 annually, making it the cheapest direct way to stream the full suite of ESPN networks. With ESPN Unlimited, you get live feeds of all of ESPN’s linear networks, including ESPN, ESPN2, ESPNU, SEC Network, ACC Network, ESPNEWS, and ESPN Deportes. It also includes all content from what was formerly known as ESPN+ (now rebranded as ESPN Select), which means you get tens of thousands of additional live events. The service is streamed through an enhanced ESPN App that includes features like Multi-view for watching up to four games at once, real-time stats, and personalized alerts. This service finally solves the long-standing confusion around ESPN+. To be clear, the cheaper ESPN Select plan ($12.99 per month) does not include a live stream of ESPN2. I cannot stress this enough: ESPN Select (formerly ESPN+) is a digital-only platform for live events, not a live cable channel subscription. If you want to stream ESPN2 or the main ESPN channel, you must subscribe to the ESPN Unlimited plan. If you are still confused about the difference, read my review of ESPN Unlimited vs ESPN Select. While there’s no direct free trial, a launch promotion bundles ESPN Unlimited with Disney+ and Hulu for the same $29.99 per month price for the first year, offering significant value. If you also want FS1, FS2 or your local FOX station, the ESPN Unlimited plan on its own won’t cover everything. That’s where the ESPN Unlimited + FOX One bundle starts to make more sense. Editor’s Pick: The ESPN Unlimited plan is easily the best deal if you insist on having ESPN2 in your channel lineup. You get the full roster of ESPN’s cable networks, and everything offered within the ESPN Select plan. That covers your channel spread to digital only networks like ESPN+, ACCNX, ESPN3 and SECN+. See all ESPN plans and bundles at ESPN. Is ESPN2 Included With ESPN+ (Now ESPN Select)? No. ESPN2 is not included with ESPN+. The service now called ESPN Select (formerly ESPN+) does not carry live cable channels like ESPN or ESPN2. It’s a separate streaming platform that focuses on live events, replays, and original shows. If you open the ESPN app with an ESPN Select subscription, you’ll see games, shows from ESPN+ and documentaries. But you won’t get a live stream of ESPN2 unless you also have a TV subscription, such as ESPN Unlimited, Sling TV, or another live TV service. The difference between ESPN’s Unlimited and Select plans is one of the biggest points of confusion I see. ESPN Select looks like it should include ESPN2, but it doesn’t. You need a plan that includes the actual ESPN cable networks to watch ESPN2 live. ESPN Unlimited + FOX One Bundle If you need ESPN2 along with FS1, FS2, and your local FOX station, but still want to cut costs, the ESPN Unlimited + FOX One bundle is your next best option. The combined services costs $39.99 per month and delivers ESPN’s full 12-network lineup across cable and digital-only channels like ESPN3, SECN+ and ACCNX. You also get all live games and on-demand shows from ESPN Select (including games on ESPN+). FOX Business, FOX Nation and FOX News are among the 11 channels under FOX One. You watch your live TV channels within the ESPN app and FOX One app. The ESPN app supports Multi-view so you can watch up to four live sporting events at once. You can get real time stats for Fantasy team owners. The biggest advantage of this bundle is how well it works with building out your channel lineup using a TV antenna. The ESPN/FOX bundle covers the major cable sports gaps, but it leaves out local NBC and CBS broadcasts. By relying on your TV antenna to pick up those local channels for free, you create a nearly complete cord-cutting sports package for a penny under $40. The bundle is highly effective for college sports fans because it gives you live games on ESPN, ESPN2, SEC Network, ACC Network, FOX and the Big Ten Network (BTN). You can read a more detailed review of the ESPN Unlimited + FOX One Bundle to learn about its channel lineup and features. The ESPN Unlimited + FOX One bundle works well if you want a tight group of sports channels. But if you’re trying to spend less each month and don’t need the full lineup, Sling TV is still the cheaper option. Editor’s Take: For anyone missing what Venu Sports could have been, the ESPN, FOX One bundle is the next best thing. It still underprices larger TV bundles, and even budget-friendly competitors like Sling TV by focusing on a core of sports cable networks. Subscribers are not only getting a cheaper price, but added blackout protection while also using a TV antenna to get local channels for free. Pick the ESPN Unlimited, FOX One bundle and start streaming. Sling TV Sling TV remains a top contender if you’re an antenna user looking for the most affordable way to add cable sports channels. For true budget streaming, Sling TV offers Sling Passes, which provide short-term access to the Sling Orange channel lineup (including ESPN2) without a monthly commitment. These prepaid passes start at $4.99 for a Day Pass (24 hours) or $9.99 for a Weekend Pass (Friday through Sunday). If you only need ESPN2 for a single major event or a playoff weekend, a Pass is usually the cheapest route. Access automatically expires, so there’s nothing to cancel. The monthly Sling Orange plan is priced at $45.99 per month. It is the cheapest multi-channel streaming bundle that includes ESPN2. This plan is great for cord-cutters who already get their local channels like ABC, CBS, and FOX for free with a TV antenna and just need to fill the cable sports gap. The Sling Orange plan provides about 32 channels, including ESPN, ESPN2, and ESPN3. Sling delivers its ESPN streams in 720p, but also offers select broadcasts, including from ESPN, in upscaled 4K at no extra cost if you have a compatible device. For more sports, you can add the Sports Extra bundle for $11 per month to get channels like ESPNU and SEC Network. While the Sling Blue plan offers local FOX, NBC and ABC stations in some major markets, its local coverage is limited. That’s why I think using a TV antenna is a great, budget-friendly approach. You can add the Sports Extra package to either Pass. It includes ESPNU and SEC Network. The add-on costs an extra $1 for a Day Pass or $2 for a Weekend Pass. Sling keeps costs down, but the trade-off is a smaller channel lineup and limited local coverage. If you want more sports channels in one place, Fubo’s sports bundle is the next step up. Find the right Sling TV package for your needs Fubo Sports & News Fubo Sports & News is a new skinny bundle for sports fans meant to drive down the cost of watching channels like ESPN2, ion and FS1. It enters the market at a promotional price of $45.99 for the first month before moving to its regular price of $55.99 per month. This skinny bundle package is designed to compete directly with other sports-focused plans and includes a pretty good lineup for the price. Fubo recently announced the ESPN Unlimited content suite is now ingested directly into the Fubo app, meaning you no longer have to use your credentials to log in to the ESPN App separately to watch ESPN2 The channel lineup includes ESPN, ESPN2, FS1, FS2, Big Ten Network, and NFL Network. FOX News is also part of the Fubo Sports & News package. The service also includes select local ABC, CBS, and FOX stations, though it notably does not carry NBC. So again, adding a TV antenna can fill in the gaps of your channel lineup without having to add another subscription. Fubo Sports includes nice features like Multiview and an unlimited Cloud DVR. Fubo’s sports bundle covers a lot of ground for the price. But if you want a more complete lineup with Turner networks like TNT and TBS, DIRECTV’s MySports plan fills in those gaps. See all plans and pricing at Fubo.tv DIRECTV The DIRECTV MySports bundle at $69.99 per month offers a focused, sports-first lineup. It includes over 25 channels, featuring ESPN, ESPN2, ESPNU, ACC Network, FS1, MLB Network, and many others. A major advantage of the MySports plan is its widespread coverage of local broadcast channels (ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX) in most U.S. markets, thanks to recent agreements with broadcasters. You also get TNT, TBS and truTV, which are needed for NHL games, the NCAA Men’s Basketball Tournament, and NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs. The channel lineup is a more complete solution than some other skinny bundles, but you are paying for it as well. DIRECTV (formerly DIRECTV STREAM) delivers high-quality streams, often in 1080p, and includes two dedicated 4K channels for certain live events. MySports comes with unlimited Cloud DVR and allows streaming on an unlimited number of devices at home. You can watch on Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV, smartphones, tablets, and most smart TVs. The service is contract-free, so you can cancel at any time. If you want regional sports networks like FanDuel Sports Network Southeast , you can add the MyHome Team package for $19.99 per month. That makes DIRECTV one of the few services where you can get ESPN2, ESPN+, and RSNs all in one place. DIRECTV also offers ESPN2 in its ENTERTAINMENT, CHOICE plans and higher-priced packages. DIRECTV gives you one of the most complete channel lineups, but it comes at a higher price. If you also want bundled streaming services like Disney+ and Hulu included, Hulu + Live TV is another option to consider. Editor’s Take: There are cheaper ways to get ESPN2. But if you do sign up for any DIRECTV package, choosing the “streaming app only” option saves money right away. You skip the $10 monthly Gemini box lease and can use your own device, such as a Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV, or Google TV Smart TV. App-only customers qualify for the 5-day free trial on signature packages like the ENTERTAINMENT plan. You also avoid the $120 per device non-return fee if you cancel later. See current DIRECTV options, including the MySports bundle. Hulu + Live TV Hulu + Live TV bundles ESPN2 with a massive on-demand library with ad-supported subscriptions to Disney+ and ESPN Unlimited. For $89.99 per month, you get over 95 live channels, including ESPN, ESPN2, SEC Network, and Big Ten Network, plus local ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX stations in most areas. The real value of this bundle is its integration with Disney’s other platforms. The price includes ad-supported subscriptions to both Disney+ and ESPN Unlimited (with ESPN Select). Hulu with Live TV comes with unlimited Cloud DVR storage. You can watch live TV on up to two screens at once. It’s a convenient and cheaper package for households that use all three services. ESPN2 streams in 720p HD, and all subscribers get unlimited Cloud DVR storage. You’ll want at least 8 to 10 Mbps of internet speed. See the latest bundles and pricing at Hulu.com YouTube TV YouTube TV offers ESPN2 in its base plan, and its new smaller sports plan. The base plan costs $82.99 per month, and has over 128 channels, including a strong sports lineup with ESPN, ESPN2, ESPNU, FS1, SEC Network, and NFL Network. It also has excellent coverage of local channels like ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX in virtually all U.S. markets. The new YouTube TV Sports Plan carries about 34 channels for $64.99 per month, including ESPN2. The Sports Plan includes ESPN, ESPN2, CBS Sports and local broadcast channels like NBC. YouTube TV is known for its clean interface and premium features, such as key play highlights and a sports multiview option. On the other hand, there are much cheaper options now just to watch ESPN networks. The service delivers ESPN streams in 1080p at 60fps. But you need to pay for the 4K Plus add-on if you want an upscaled 4K picture. You get unlimited Cloud DVR. An internet download speed of 10 to 15 Mbps (or more) of bandwidth is recommended. Unlike the Hulu bundle, YouTube TV does not include ESPN Unlimited or Disney+. And now that we are in the skinny bundle era, it raises the question whether you need to be spending $83 per month just to watch football or basketball. YouTube TV is supported across most Smart TVs and major streaming devices, including Google TV, Roku, Fire TV, NVIDIA Shield TV, Apple TV. See plans and pricing at tv.youtube.com How a TV Antenna Completes Your Cord-Cutting Setup As I always say here at Antenna Land, the foundation of any smart cord-cutting strategy is a TV antenna. While services like ESPN Unlimited and Sling TV are essential for cable channels like ESPN2, they don’t cover everything. Major sporting events, from the NFL on CBS and FOX to the NBA Finals on ABC, are broadcast live over the public airwaves for free. By using a streaming service for ESPN2 with a TV antenna, you create a complete and cost-effective setup without spending $80 or more per month. You can even add a DVR for antenna channels, and start recording whatever you like. You pay a small monthly fee for the specific sports channels you can’t get otherwise, and you rely on your antenna for free access to your local network channels. This saves you from paying for expensive “cable replacement” services that charge you for local channels you could be getting for free. For example, a service like Sling Orange gets you ESPN2, but it has limited local channel coverage under the Sling Blue plan. A TV antenna fills that gap for a one-time cost. Even with a more comprehensive bundle like DIRECTV’s MySports plan, which now includes many local stations, a TV antenna is still a good idea. You get your own reliable source for local channels, including some like MeTV, ion, or COMET that are not included in your subscription. Antenna channels have far less compression than cable or streaming so you are getting the best possible picture quality, especially in NEXTGEN TV (ATSC 3.0) markets where you can get 1080p HDR broadcasts. Frequently Asked Questions About Watching ESPN2 Here are answers to some other common questions that come up when trying to watch ESPN2 without cable. What streaming services have ESPN and ESPN2 in 2026? In 2026, you can get both ESPN and ESPN2 on several services, but I recommend using a skinny bundle. The cheapest option is ESPN Unlimited ($29.99 per month). Other “skinny bundle” options include the new Fubo Sports & News package ($55.99 per month after promo) and DIRECTV MySports ($69.99 per month). Sling TV (Orange Plan, $45.99 per month), Hulu + Live TV ($82.99 per month), and YouTube TV ($82.99 per month) also include both channels in their base plans. Can I watch ESPN2 for free? No, you cannot watch ESPN2 for free legally. It is a cable channel that requires a paid subscription to a streaming service or a cable/satellite package. The only way to watch sports for free is by using a TV antenna to pick up local broadcast channels like ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX. Can you watch ESPN2 on ESPN+ (now ESPN Select)? No. This is a major point of confusion for users. The service now called ESPN Select (formerly ESPN+) has never included the live linear ESPN2 channel. To stream the live ESPN2 channel directly from ESPN, you can subscribe to the ESPN Unlimited plan. March 2026 update: I added new sections to clarify the cheapest way to watch ESPN2 and whether it’s available for free. I also updated the guide to better explain the difference between ESPN Unlimited and ESPN Select, and improved comparisons between streaming options so you can make a quicker decision.
